passage:
All December, Yuki watched the windows on her street in Uppsala fill with candle-bridges and paper stars. Her family had moved from Osaka in August. At school everyone talked about Lucia morning and saffron buns, and Yuki nodded, understanding the words but not the feeling. Walking home, she counted lit windows; theirs was the only dark one.
On the thirteenth, Anders from next door knocked, holding a paper bag. 'My mum says come for Lucia breakfast. Your whole family. Bring nothing.' Yuki's mother bowed twice at the door. The next morning Yuki sat in a warm kitchen, a saffron bun in each hand, while Anders's little sister taught her the song.

qa.q: Where had Yuki's family moved from?
qa.a: From Osaka.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling as she counted lit windows on the way home?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left out, noticing that her home was the only dark window on the street.

qa.q: Why did Anders's invitation matter so much?
qa.a: It was simple and cost little, but it brought the whole family inside the festival instead of watching from outside.

qa.q: How might Anders's family have felt hosting Yuki's family for Lucia?
qa.a: They probably felt glad and warm, sharing their tradition and helping new neighbours feel at home.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a migrant family who feels outside the neighbours' festival until a simple invitation from next door brings her in.

passage:
In Class 9 at the Lucknow school, Diwali week meant rangoli contests, diya painting and talk of whose house would have the best lights. Sabina, fourteen, new since July, painted her diya carefully but ate lunch alone while the others planned visits. Her family was the only Christian one on their lane, and no one had knocked yet.
On Thursday, Nandini slid onto the bench beside her. 'Come to our place on Diwali evening? Ma makes the best kaju katli. And my Nani wants to meet the girl who painted that peacock diya.'
Sabina blinked. 'Really?'
'Really. Bring your brother too.'
For the first time that week, Sabina laughed out loud.

qa.q: What did Sabina paint on the diya?
qa.a: A peacock.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling while eating lunch alone during Diwali week?
qa.a: She felt lonely and outside, watching the others plan visits while her family had no invitations yet.

qa.q: What could other classmates learn from Nandini?
qa.a: That a simple, warm invitation to a new student costs little and can make a huge difference.

qa.q: How might Nandini's Nani feel meeting Sabina on Diwali?
qa.a: Nani would likely feel pleased and welcoming, eager to meet the girl whose diya impressed her.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager from a minority family who feels outside while classmates celebrate, and how a friend's invitation makes a large difference at little cost.

passage:
Every Navratri the whole lane in the small town of Bardoli danced garba under the lights, and every year Zubin, fifteen, watched from his balcony. His family was the only Parsi one on the street. Nobody had ever said he couldn't come. Nobody had ever said he could.

This year Manjula Aunty from across the lane looked up and caught him watching. She marched upstairs, knocked, and held out a folded kediyu. "My son's old one. Come down. Circle three is slow, for beginners."

Zubin went red. "I don't know the steps."

"Nobody does, the first night."

He went. He was terrible. Manjula Aunty's son laughed and pulled him into the circle anyway. By the ninth night he knew the claps.

qa.q: What did Manjula Aunty hold out?
qa.a: She held out a folded kediyu, her son's old one.

qa.q: How had Zubin felt watching from the balcony every year?
qa.a: Zubin felt left out and lonely, never told he couldn't come but never invited either.

qa.q: What made the difference for Zubin?
qa.a: A simple, direct invitation with an outfit and a beginners' circle, which cost Manjula Aunty very little.

qa.q: How might Manjula Aunty feel seeing Zubin keep time by the ninth night?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and warm, glad she finally knocked on his door.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a minority family watching neighbours' festival from outside until a simple invitation brings him in.

passage:
On the evening of the Three Kings parade in Madrid, Kofi, fourteen, stood at the edge of the crowd with his hands in his pockets. The floats threw sweets; children screamed with delight. His family had arrived from Kumasi only in August, and nobody had explained why everyone was so excited about kings in January.

Santiago spotted him and pushed through the crowd. "You came! Tomorrow you come to my grandmother's for roscón. There's a little figure hidden in it. Whoever finds it is king for the day."

"Is that allowed? I'm not family."

"My abuela invites everybody. Bring your sister."

The next day Kofi's sister found the figure in her slice. The whole table cheered her in Spanish, and Kofi, laughing, translated it into Twi.

qa.q: Where had Kofi's family arrived from?
qa.a: His family had arrived from Kumasi only in August.

qa.q: How did Kofi feel at the edge of the crowd?
qa.a: Kofi felt like an outsider, hands in his pockets, not understanding why everyone was so excited.

qa.q: Why did Santiago's invitation matter so much?
qa.a: It cost almost nothing, yet it explained the custom and gave Kofi and his sister a seat at the table.

qa.q: How might Santiago's abuela see welcoming Kofi's family?
qa.a: She seems to enjoy welcoming everybody, seeing new guests as part of the fun.

grounding: Shows a migrant teenager feeling outside a local festival until a friend's small invitation brings his family in.

passage:
At the school in Chennai the corridor was decorated for Pongal, and Class 9 was drawing kolams in the courtyard. Baljeet, fifteen, the only Sikh boy in the school, sat on the steps with his sketchbook. His family had moved from Ludhiana two years ago. At home, Gurpurab had just passed with nobody at school noticing.

Devika ma'am, the class teacher, sat down beside him. "Not drawing?"

"It's not my festival, ma'am."

She thought for a moment. "Would you draw the kolam with Selvi's group? And for Gurpurab next year, would you tell the class what your family does? I'd like to know too."

Selvi waved him over and handed him the chalk. "Make the middle. I'm bad at circles."

Baljeet was good at circles.

qa.q: Where had Baljeet's family moved from?
qa.a: His family had moved from Ludhiana two years ago.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel sitting on the steps?
qa.a: Baljeet felt left out and a bit lonely, since his own festival had passed unnoticed and the Pongal fun felt like someone else's.

qa.q: What small invitations helped Baljeet join in?
qa.a: Devika ma'am's offer to join a kolam group and to share Gurpurab next year, and Selvi handing him the chalk.

qa.q: How might Selvi feel when Baljeet draws the circle?
qa.a: Selvi likely feels glad and impressed, since she is bad at circles and he is good at them.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a minority family feeling outside a school festival, and small invitations from a teacher and classmate bringing him in.

passage:
Dear Varun,
It's Diwali week in our colony again, and it's strange without you. You know how it was before you moved: every balcony full of lights, crackers, sweet boxes going door to door, and our flat dark. We're Tibetan; Losar is in February, and nobody here has heard of it. For years I sat inside with the curtains shut, feeling like we lived in a different country.
Then you knocked, three Diwalis ago, and dragged me down to light diyas with your family. Your mother gave me kaju katli and said, "Next year, you bring something from your festival." I still remember how warm that felt.
This year, guess what. Mrs Rao from 3B knocked. "Tenzin, come for Lakshmi puja. Bring your mother." We went. My mother brought khapse, our Losar biscuits. Everyone ate them all.
I'm inviting the whole floor for Losar. You're invited too, even from Pune.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Tenzin's mother bring to the Lakshmi puja?
qa.a: Khapse, their Losar biscuits.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel during Diwali before Varun's invitation?
qa.a: Tenzin felt left out and lonely, sitting inside with the curtains shut as if living in a different country.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's story show about invitations?
qa.a: A simple invitation from a friend or neighbour costs little but can make someone from a minority family feel part of the community.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt when everyone ate the khapse?
qa.a: She probably felt glad and warm, happy that her invitation brought Tenzin's family and their festival into the colony.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager from a minority migrant family who feels outside neighbours' festivals, and how invitations make a big difference.
